edges.effect_quant: The breast-cancer literature suggests a modest protective association for higher whole-grain intake, but the signal is less settled than for colorectal cancer.
edges.mechanism: Whole grains may reduce insulin-related signaling, improve fiber fermentation, and shift overall dietary quality in ways that could modestly affect hormone-sensitive carcinogenesis. The likely effect is small, but the biologic direction is coherent with broader plant-rich diet findings.
edges.summary: The direct observational meta-analysis found lower breast-cancer risk with higher whole-grain intake, and later food-group syntheses kept whole grains on the protective side of the evidence map. The effect is not strong enough to treat as a headline intervention on its own, but it is consistent with a broader pattern favoring minimally refined carbohydrate sources.
edges.caveats: This is observational nutrition evidence, so healthy-user bias and correlated food-pattern confounding remain major limitations. The colorectal-cancer signal for whole grains is stronger than the breast-cancer one, so confidence here should stay moderate rather than high.
